project.title: Why Your Phone Battery Gets Worse Every Year
project.topic: How lithium-ion battery chemistry gradually loses capacity with charge cycles, heat, and age
project.script: Your phone battery can show one hundred percent and still hold less energy than it did when it was new. Most phones use lithium-ion batteries, where ions move between two electrodes as the battery charges and discharges. Over time, side reactions consume some of the materials that store energy, so the battery's maximum capacity slowly shrinks. Heat speeds up that aging, and keeping a battery at very high or very low charge for long periods can add stress. That's why an older phone may need charging earlier in the day. The battery isn't suddenly broken; its chemistry has gradually changed.

project.title: How GPS Works When Your Phone Has No Internet
project.topic: How satellite navigation calculates location and why maps may still need downloaded data
project.script: Your phone can often find its location even when the internet is off. GPS satellites continuously broadcast the time and their positions. Your phone listens to several satellites and compares when each signal arrived, using the tiny timing differences to estimate how far away each satellite is. With enough signals, it calculates a position on Earth. The internet is useful for loading maps, traffic, and search results, but it isn't what makes GPS positioning work. If you download a map in advance, navigation can keep working offline, although live traffic and online searches won't.

project.title: What Really Happens When You Delete a File?
project.topic: How file systems mark storage as available and why deleted data can sometimes be recovered
project.script: When you delete a file, your computer often doesn't immediately erase every bit of its contents. It usually removes the file's directory entry and marks the storage space as available for reuse. Until that space is overwritten, some data may remain recoverable. But solid-state drives complicate the story: a feature called TRIM can tell the drive which blocks are no longer needed, and the drive may clear them during internal cleanup. That's why deleting a file isn't the same as securely wiping it. If information is sensitive, use a trusted secure-erasure method appropriate for the device.

project.title: Why Airplane Routes Look Curved on a Flat Map
project.topic: Why great-circle routes can look bent when Earth's curved surface is projected onto a flat map
project.script: Look at a world map and some airplane routes seem to take a strange detour toward the north. Often, they're following a shorter path, not a longer one. Earth is roughly spherical, and the shortest route between two points on a sphere follows a great-circle path. When that curved surface is flattened into a map, the route can look bent because the map projection distorts distances and directions. Real flight plans also account for winds, weather, airspace, and safety. So the line you see on a flat screen isn't always the path that looks straight to your eyes.

project.title: How an Airplane's Black Box Survives a Crash
project.topic: What flight data and cockpit voice recorders do and how crash-protected recorders are designed
project.script: An airplane's black box is usually bright orange, not black, because investigators need to find it. Most modern aircraft carry a flight data recorder and a cockpit voice recorder. One records information such as altitude, speed, and control inputs; the other captures cockpit audio. The recording units are built inside protective cases designed to withstand severe impact, heat, and pressure. Underwater locator beacons can help search teams find them after an accident at sea. They don't prevent crashes, but they preserve evidence that helps investigators understand what happened and improve aviation safety.
